summary: Stellarys is health monitoring software for astronauts on missions where Earth can’t answer in time. In January 2026, Crew-11 carried out the first medical evacuation from the ISS. From Mars, that option won’t exist, and a single message can take up to 22 minutes one way. We developed a prototype that gives crews clinical autonomy, with no need for an external connection. Each astronaut wears a layered sensor kit: a sensor shirt, a glucose monitor and a dosimeter, plus spot-check devices such as the 1DROP blood reader. A local server on the spacecraft runs a rules engine that compares every reading with the crew member’s personal baseline and with absolute safety limits. It then rates them Fit, Fit with restrictions or Unfit. An onboard small language model explains each finding in plain language and points to the protocol to follow. A 3D visual twin shows each body zone in green, amber or red. When a crew member’s fitness drops, an algorithm proposes redistributing their tasks for the commander to approve. The history syncs with the flight surgeon on Earth whenever there is a link. Stellarys connects health with operations, so crews can act early and safely without waiting for Earth.
details:
Stellarys is onboard health monitoring software for astronauts. It works without an external connection, so crews can detect health changes early, know what to do and reorganize their work without waiting for Earth.

Each crew member wears a layered sensor kit. The always-worn layer is a textile sensor shirt (Bio-Monitor/Astroskin type), a continuous glucose monitor and a personal dosimeter. Other devices are worn at times, such as a blood pressure cuff and a core temperature sensor. Shared devices are used for spot checks: a pulse oximeter, a tonometer for SANS surveillance, a 1DROP-type blood reader and a tablet for reaction tests, mood and symptoms. The data reach a local server in each spacecraft, station or base over Bluetooth Low Energy.

On that server, a clinical rules engine compares every reading with the crew member's personal baseline and with absolute safety limits. It then rates each person Fit, Fit with restrictions or Unfit. A stress and fatigue index from 0 to 100 is based on NASA's Reaction Self Test research. A small language model running on board explains each finding in plain language, always in the same order: what we saw, what it may mean, what to do now, when to escalate, and which rule triggered it. The SLM does not decide alerts. The rules detect, the SLM explains, and a person decides.

A 3D visual twin shows each body zone in green, amber or red. Alerts arrive by wearable vibration, by tablet, or by habitat-wide voice in emergencies. When a crew member's fitness drops, a replanning algorithm weighs each pending task's criticality, duration and required certifications against the status of the rest of the crew. It then proposes a safe redistribution for the commander or crew medical officer to approve. The history syncs with the flight surgeon on Earth over delay-tolerant networking whenever there is a link.

Benefits and intended impact
Stellarys gives deep-space crews (Artemis, Gateway, Mars) autonomy during communication delays of up to 22 minutes one way and during blackouts. It reduces errors caused by fatigue or illness and gives flight surgeons structured, auditable histories. In low Earth orbit, it means continuous monitoring with less time spent on manual measurements. The same approach could also serve isolated settings on Earth, such as Antarctic bases, offshore platforms and rural health centers like many in Nicaragua.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React, Vite and Tailwind CSS.
  • Backend: Python with FastAPI, Uvicorn and Pydantic, with SQLite for history.
  • Visual twin: our own 3D astronaut model, built and animated in Blender and rendered on the web with Three.js.
  • Other tools: Canva for the document design, Claude and Claude Code to organize sources and speed up programming, and NotebookLM to gather sources.

The working web prototype simulates a three-person crew with Nominal, Stress and Critical scenarios. It also includes an Earth Control view for the flight surgeon and environment profiles for the space station, spacecraft in transit, lunar base and planetary rover. All data are synthetic, generated from ranges in NASA's open literature.

Creativity
Existing projects like CMO-DA and HERMES help diagnose or manage health data. Stellarys connects health status with mission operations, so a fatigued or ill astronaut is not assigned critical tasks. It also adapts its behavior to each environment, including escalation paths, active rules, radiation alerts and medication tracking. The visual twin makes medical status understandable at a glance for crew members who are not physicians.

Factors we considered

  • Communication latency.
  • AI reliability: verifiable rules make the critical decisions, with human approval.
  • Medical privacy: each role sees only what it needs.
  • Comfort of all-day sensors and gray for missing data, so it is never mistaken for "all good."
  • NASA-STD-3001 and the five HRP hazards.
  • Known limitations: clinical validation is still pending, microgravity affects sensor accuracy, and radiation can degrade the electronics.
